course: Daily Bread Sales: Bakery Production System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Bread is a daily staple in many African households, and small bakeries can thrive by selling fresh loaves at affordable prices. But without a consistent recipe and proper scaling, your bread will vary in taste, size, and qualityâcustomers will notice and may not return. This module teaches you how to use a standard bread recipe and scale it up or down accurately, so you can produce the same great bread every day, whether you bake 10 loaves or 100.

Why does scaling matter? If you double a recipe by simply doubling all ingredients, you might run into problems: dough that's too stiff or too soft, bread that doesn't rise properly, or inconsistent baking times. Professional bakers use baker's percentages, where flour is always 100%, and other ingredients are a percentage of the flour weight. This makes scaling easy and precise. For example, if your recipe calls for 1000g flour, 600g water (60%), 20g salt (2%), and 10g yeast (1%), you can scale to any flour weight by multiplying.

In Africa, ingredients like flour, yeast, and salt are available in most markets, but prices fluctuate. Accurate scaling reduces waste and controls costs. If you know exactly how much dough each loaf requires, you can calculate your cost per loaf and set a profitable price. Also, consistent size and quality build trustâcustomers will come back for your reliable bread.

This module will guide you through tools, step-by-step methods, common mistakes, safety, and a practical exercise. By the end, you'll be able to write your own scalable bread recipe and produce uniform loaves that sell. Remember, baking is a skill that improves with practice, and mastering scaling is the foundation of a successful bakery business.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To bake bread consistently and scale recipes, you need the right tools and materials. Most are affordable and available in local markets or online. First, a digital kitchen scale is essential. It should measure in grams, up to at least 5kg. A scale ensures accuracyâvolume measures like cups are not precise enough for scaling. You can find digital scales in supermarkets or electronics shops for around $10-$20.

Next, you need large mixing bowls. Plastic or stainless steel bowls work well. For scaling up, you might need a very large bowl or a clean plastic basin. A sturdy wooden spoon or a dough scraper helps mix and handle dough. If you plan to bake many loaves, consider a dough mixer, but for small-scale, hand mixing is fine. You'll also need measuring spoons for small amounts like yeast and salt, though a scale is better.

For shaping and proofing, you need loaf pans. Standard loaf pans are about 9x5 inches. If you don't have pans, you can shape round loaves and bake on a tray. Parchment paper or greased trays prevent sticking. A clean cloth or plastic wrap is needed to cover dough while it rises. A thermometer is useful to check water temperatureâyeast works best at 25-30Â°C. If you don't have a thermometer, use lukewarm water (comfortable to touch).

An oven is the biggest investment. If you don't have a commercial oven, a home oven or even a charcoal oven can work. You'll need a baking stone or a heavy tray for even heat. A spray bottle for water helps create steam for a crispy crust. Finally, keep a notebook to record your recipes and scaling calculations. This helps you replicate successful batches. In Africa, you can source these tools locally: markets sell bowls and pans, and hardware stores have scales. Start with basics and upgrade as your business grows.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Follow these steps to scale and bake bread consistently. Start with a basic recipe: 1000g bread flour, 600g water (60%), 20g salt (2%), 10g instant yeast (1%). This makes about 2 large loaves (each around 800g dough). To scale, decide how many loaves you want. For 10 loaves, multiply all ingredients by 5: 5000g flour, 3000g water, 100g salt, 50g yeast.

Step 1: Weigh all ingredients accurately using your scale. Use warm water (25-30Â°C). Step 2: In a large bowl, mix flour and salt. In another bowl, dissolve yeast in water. Pour yeast mixture into flour and mix with a spoon until a shaggy dough forms. Step 3: Turn dough onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 10-15 minutes until smooth and elastic. If scaling up, knead in batches or use a mixer. Step 4: Place dough in a greased bowl, cover, and let rise until doubled in size, about 1-2 hours depending on room temperature. In hot African climates, rising may be faster, so check after 45 minutes.

Step 5: Punch down dough and divide into equal pieces. For 800g loaves, weigh each piece. Shape into balls, then flatten and roll into loaf shapes. Place in greased loaf pans. Step 6: Cover and proof again until dough rises just above the pan, about 30-45 minutes. Step 7: Preheat oven to 220Â°C (425Â°F). If using a home oven, preheat with a baking stone or tray. Step 8: Bake for 30-35 minutes until golden brown and hollow-sounding when tapped. For steam, place a pan of water in the oven or spray loaves with water before baking. Step 9: Remove from pans and cool on a wire rack. Cooling is important for texture. Now you can repeat this process with any scale, ensuring consistent results.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Even experienced bakers make mistakes. Here are common issues when scaling bread recipes and how to fix them. Mistake 1: Not using a scale. Volume measurements like cups vary, leading to inconsistent dough. Fix: Always weigh ingredients in grams. If you don't have a scale, use a known container to calibrate, but invest in a scale soon.

Mistake 2: Incorrect water temperature. Too hot water kills yeast; too cold slows fermentation. Fix: Use lukewarm water (25-30Â°C). If you don't have a thermometer, test on your wristâit should feel neither hot nor cold. Mistake 3: Over-scaling without adjusting mixing time. When you double or triple a recipe, mixing and kneading take longer. Fix: Knead until dough is smooth and elastic, regardless of time. If using a mixer, watch for dough climbing the hook.

Mistake 4: Not adjusting rising time for climate. In hot African regions, dough rises faster. Fix: Check dough after 30 minutes; if doubled, proceed. In cold weather, rising may take longerâfind a warm spot. Mistake 5: Inaccurate division. Uneven loaves bake unevenly. Fix: Weigh each piece of dough. Use a scale to ensure equal weight. Mistake 6: Skipping steam. Steam gives a crispy crust and better rise. Fix: Place a metal pan with water in the oven, or spray loaves with water before baking.

Mistake 7: Underbaking. Bread may look done but be raw inside. Fix: Use a thermometerâinternal temperature should be 90-95Â°C. Or tap the bottom; it should sound hollow. Mistake 8: Not cooling properly. Cutting hot bread leads to gummy texture. Fix: Cool completely on a wire rack before slicing. Mistake 9: Stale ingredients. Old yeast or flour gives poor results. Fix: Store ingredients in airtight containers and check expiration dates. By avoiding these mistakes, your scaled bread will be consistent and sellable.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Baking involves heat, sharp tools, and electrical equipment, so safety is crucial. Always wash your hands before handling food. Keep your work area clean and sanitized. When using an oven, use oven mitts to avoid burns. Never leave hot pans unattended. If using a gas oven, check for leaks regularly. For charcoal ovens, ensure proper ventilation to avoid carbon monoxide buildup.

Handle knives and dough scrapers carefully. Cut away from your body. Store knives safely when not in use. If using a dough mixer, keep hands away from moving parts. Unplug before cleaning. Also, be mindful of electrical safety: don't use wet hands to plug or unplug appliances. Keep cords away from water.

Best practices for scaling: Always write down your scaled recipe and keep records. This helps you replicate success and adjust for cost. Use baker's percentages to easily scale up or down. For example, if you want to use 2kg of flour, calculate water as 60% of 2000g = 1200g, salt 2% = 40g, yeast 1% = 20g. This method works for any amount.

Maintain a clean workspace. Clean as you go to prevent cross-contamination. Store ingredients properly: flour in a cool, dry place; yeast in the fridge or freezer for longer shelf life. Label containers with dates. When baking for sale, follow local health regulations. Wear clean aprons and hairnets if required. Practice good personal hygiene. Finally, don't rush. Baking is a science; accurate measurements and patience yield the best results. By following these safety and best practices, you'll produce safe, high-quality bread that customers trust.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now it's time to practice scaling and baking. For this exercise, you will scale a basic bread recipe to make 6 loaves of about 800g each. Start with the standard recipe: 1000g flour, 600g water, 20g salt, 10g yeast. Calculate the total dough weight: 1000+600+20+10 = 1630g. This makes about 2 loaves of 800g (with a little extra). To make 6 loaves, you need 6 x 800g = 4800g dough. Scale factor = 4800 / 1630 â 2.94. Round to 3 for simplicity. So multiply all ingredients by 3: 3000g flour, 1800g water, 60g salt, 30g yeast. Total dough = 3000+1800+60+30 = 4890g, which makes 6 loaves of about 815g each.

Now, gather your tools: scale, large bowl, spoon, loaf pans, oven. Weigh ingredients accurately. Mix and knead as described in Lesson 3. Let dough rise until doubled. Divide into 6 equal pieces (weigh each to be precise). Shape into loaves and place in pans. Proof until risen. Bake at 220Â°C for 30-35 minutes. Cool on racks.

After baking, evaluate your loaves: Are they uniform in size? Did they rise well? Taste a slice. Record your observations. Calculate cost: if flour costs $1 per kg, water negligible, salt and yeast minimal, your total cost for 6 loaves is about $3.50. If you sell each loaf for $1.50, your profit is $9 - $3.50 = $5.50. Adjust pricing based on local market.

Repeat the exercise with a different scale, say for 12 loaves, to practice. Try using baker's percentages: for 5000g flour, water = 3000g, salt = 100g, yeast = 50g. This makes about 10 loaves. Practice until you can scale confidently. This skill will save you time and money, and ensure consistent quality for your customers.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Bread Recipes and Scaling

This practical reference is your bench-side companion for the Bread Recipes and Scaling module in Daily Bread Sales: Bakery Production System. In an African bakery business, scaling is not just arithmetic â it is the difference between a consistent product that customers return for and a batch that loses you money. Whether you are baking in Lagos, Accra, Nairobi, or a rural growth centre, the principle is the same: recipes are formulas, and scaling is the business discipline that turns a formula into profit.

Use this reference alongside the lessons on Tools and Materials, Step by Step Method, Common Mistakes and Fixes, Safety and Best Practice, and your Practical Exercise. Print it, laminate it, and pin it near your mixing bench.

Why Baker's Percentage Beats Cup Measuring

Volume measuring (cups, spoons) is unreliable because flour compacts differently depending on humidity, storage, and how it was scooped. In many African markets, flour is sold in 50 kg bags whose moisture content varies with the rainy or dry season. Baker's percentage removes this guesswork. Once you fix flour at 100%, every other ingredient is a percentage of that weight. Scaling then becomes a single multiplication â the "scale factor" â applied to every ingredient.

Business-first insight: the same formula lets you calculate cost per loaf, forecast flour purchases, and price your bread without guessing. A bakery that cannot scale accurately cannot quote a contract for 500 loaves to a school, hotel, or supermarket.

Standard Bread Formula Reference

The table below shows a typical lean African white bread dough (no added fat), which is the workhorse of daily bread sales. Adjust water for local flour absorption.

Table 1: Lean White Bread Formula (Baker's Percentage)
Ingredient Baker's % Weight for 1 kg flour (g) Weight for 10 kg flour (kg) Function
Wheat flour (bread)100%100010.0Structure, gluten
Water60%6006.0Hydration, gluten development
Instant yeast2%200.20Fermentation
Salt1.8%180.18Flavour, gluten strengthening
Sugar4%400.40Yeast food, crust colour
Vegetable oil (optional)3%300.30Softness, shelf life
Total dough170.8%170817.08â

Source: Formula structure based on the baker's percentage conventions published by the Bread Bakers Guild of America (bbga.org) and the ingredient ratios in King Arthur Baking Company's free "Baker's Percentage" resource (kingarthurbaking.com). Water percentage should be adjusted to local flour quality â African hard wheat often absorbs 58â64%.

Yield and Scaling Table

To scale, multiply every ingredient by the scale factor. The table below shows how many 500 g dough pieces (roughly 450 g baked loaves) you get from different flour weights.

Table 2: Scaling Factors and Loaf Yield

Source: Yield calculations based on the dough yield method described by the American Institute of Baking and the Bread Bakers Guild of America formula scaling guidance (bbga.org). Yield assumes 2% processing loss, typical in small African bakeries.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Scaling and Dough Handling

Never scale dough or ingredients on the same surface used for raw meat, poultry, or eggs. Flour dust is a respiratory hazard â wear a dust mask when handling 50 kg bags, and tie bags securely to prevent weevil and rodent contamination. Use food-grade, calibrated scales only; a broken scale can mean under-salted dough (poor shelf life) or over-yeasted dough (collapsed loaves). When scaling hot water, keep it below 60Â°C to protect yeast and avoid burns. Store yeast away from strong odours and moisture â in African humid climates, opened yeast must be resealed and refrigerated within 24 hours.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Calibrate your scale before every batch â use a known 1 kg weight or a sealed bag of salt.
  2. Convert the recipe to baker's percentage with flour always at 100%.
  3. Decide your flour weight first â this is your anchor, not the number of loaves.
  4. Multiply every ingredient by the same scale factor â never scale one ingredient alone.
  5. Check water temperature against flour temperature to hit a final dough temperature of 24â26Â°C.
  6. Record actual weights and yields in a batch log for costing and consistency.
  7. Adjust water by 1â2% if the flour is new or the weather has changed.
  8. Weigh dough pieces individually â equal pieces bake evenly and sell fairly.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • King Arthur Baking Company â Baker's Percentage Guide (free, beginner-friendly).
  • Bread Bakers Guild of America â Formula and Scaling Resources (free articles and standards).
  • FAO â Small-Scale Bread Baking and Food Safety Guidelines (free PDFs on bakery hygiene and grain handling).
  • U.S. FDA â Food Safety for Bakeries (free reference for scaling, storage, and sanitation).
  • Institute of Food Science & Technology â Bread and Bakery Science (free fact sheets).

Prepared for Daily Bread Sales: Bakery Production System â Rise AFRICA Skills. This practical reference is for training use; always follow your national food safety authority's regulations.

quiz.q: Why is scaling important in bread baking?
options: A) It makes bread taste better.
B) It ensures consistent quality and controls costs.
D) It eliminates the need for yeast.
quiz.explanation: Scaling ensures each loaf is the same size and quality, and helps calculate accurate costs.

quiz.q: What is the baker's percentage for flour in a standard bread recipe?
quiz.explanation: In baker's percentages, flour is always 100%, and other ingredients are a percentage of the flour weight.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for accurate scaling?
quiz.explanation: A digital scale measures in grams, ensuring precise ingredient amounts for scaling.

quiz.q: What is the ideal water temperature for activating yeast?
quiz.explanation: Yeast works best at lukewarm temperatures around 25-30Â°C.

quiz.q: How can you check if bread is fully baked?
options: A) Tap the top; it should sound hollow.
B) Insert a toothpick; it should come out clean.
quiz.explanation: Both tapping the bottom for a hollow sound and checking internal temperature indicate doneness.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when scaling a recipe?
quiz.explanation: When scaling up, mixing and kneading take longer, so you must adjust time accordingly.

quiz.q: Why is steam important in baking bread?
options: A) It makes the crust crispy and helps rise.
B) It adds moisture to the dough.
quiz.explanation: Steam creates a crispy crust and allows the bread to expand fully before crust sets.

quiz.q: What should you do if your dough rises too quickly in a hot climate?
options: A) Put it in the fridge.
B) Check after 30 minutes and proceed if doubled.
quiz.explanation: In hot climates, dough rises faster, so monitor and proceed when doubled to avoid over-proofing.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safety practice when baking?
options: C) Using wet hands to plug appliances
quiz.explanation: Oven mitts protect hands from burns when handling hot pans.

quiz.q: How do you calculate the amount of water for 2000g of flour at 60% hydration?
What is the first step in the bread-making process?
quiz.explanation: Dissolving yeast in water first ensures even distribution before mixing with dry ingredients.

quiz.q: Why is it important to cool bread before slicing?
quiz.explanation: Cutting hot bread can make it gummy because the internal structure is still setting.

quiz.q: What does a dough scraper help with?
quiz.explanation: A dough scraper is used to lift, fold, and divide dough cleanly.

quiz.q: If you want to bake 4 loaves of 800g each, what total dough weight do you need?
quiz.explanation: 4 loaves Ã 800g = 3200g total dough.

quiz.q: What should you do if your bread is underbaked?
options: A) Return it to the oven for a few more minutes.
B) Increase the temperature and bake longer.
C) Cover with foil and bake.
quiz.explanation: Returning to the oven for additional time is the simplest fix for underbaked bread.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records of your scaled recipes?
options: A) To replicate success and adjust costs.
D) To avoid buying new tools.
quiz.explanation: Records help you consistently produce the same product and calculate accurate pricing.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of proofing dough?
options: A) To let it rise before baking.
D) To make it easier to shape.
quiz.explanation: Proofing allows the dough to rise and develop texture before baking.

quiz.q: Which ingredient is typically 2% of flour weight in a standard bread recipe?
quiz.explanation: Salt is usually 2% of the flour weight in baker's percentages.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when using a dough mixer?
options: A) Keep hands away from moving parts.
C) Use wet hands to operate.
quiz.explanation: Keeping hands away from moving parts prevents injury.

quiz.q: How can you create steam in a home oven?
options: A) Place a pan of water in the oven.
B) Spray loaves with water before baking.
D) Open the oven door frequently.
quiz.explanation: Both methods introduce steam to the oven environment.

quiz.q: What is the scaled amount of yeast for 3000g flour if the original recipe uses 1% yeast?
quiz.explanation: 1% of 3000g is 30g.

quiz.q: Why is it important to weigh dough pieces before shaping?
options: A) To ensure uniform loaf size.
quiz.explanation: Weighing ensures each loaf is the same size, which leads to even baking and consistent pricing.

quiz.q: What should you do if your dough is too sticky?
options: A) Add more flour, a little at a time.
D) Knead longer without adding anything.
quiz.explanation: Adding flour gradually can fix sticky dough without making it too dry.

quiz.q: Which of these is a best practice for storing yeast?
options: A) Keep in a warm place.
B) Store in the fridge or freezer.
quiz.explanation: Yeast stays active longer when stored in a cool, dry place like the fridge or freezer.

quiz.q: What is the total dough weight for the standard recipe (1000g flour, 600g water, 20g salt, 10g yeast)?
quiz.explanation: Summing all ingredients: 1000+600+20+10 = 1630g.

quiz.q: Why is it important to preheat the oven?
options: A) To ensure even baking from the start.
quiz.explanation: Preheating ensures the oven is at the correct temperature when the dough goes in, leading to proper rise and crust.

quiz.q: What is the recommended internal temperature for baked bread?
quiz.explanation: Bread is fully baked when its internal temperature reaches 90-95Â°C.

quiz.q: What should you do before slicing bread?
quiz.explanation: Cooling completely prevents gummy texture and allows proper slicing.

quiz.q: How can you calculate the cost per loaf?
options: A) Divide total ingredient cost by number of loaves.
B) Multiply cost by number of loaves.
C) Estimate based on market price.
quiz.explanation: Dividing total cost by the number of loaves gives the cost per loaf for accurate pricing.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of using baker's percentages?
options: A) Easy scaling up or down.
quiz.explanation: Baker's percentages allow you to easily adjust recipe quantities while maintaining proportions.
